title: Is that orbit really oval?
hook: Tilt a circular orbit and watch its apparent shape change.
misconception: An orbit that looks oval from one view must be an elliptical orbit.
objective: Explain that tilting a circular orbit changes its projected shape while its actual radius and speed stay fixed in the stated model.

claims.text: The stage shows a circular orbit tilted about its horizontal axis and viewed with orthographic projection.
claims.source: Demo.tsx projects (R cos(a), R sin(a) cos(tilt)) at R = 95 display units.

claims.text: The projected short axis is multiplied by cos(tilt); at 60 degrees it is half as long.
claims.source: Rotation about x followed by projection onto x-y: (R cos(a), R sin(a) cos(tilt)); cos(60 degrees) = 1/2.

claims.text: In the stated model the circle's orientation changes without changing its radius or constant speed.
claims.source: Explicit model assumption: rigidly reorient the same circular orbit, holding its physical radius and speed constant.

claims.text: A circular ring viewed at an angle can look oval while remaining circular.
claims.source: The orthographic projection described in physics.inclined-orbit-projection.axis.

recall.question: A circular ring looks oval when you tilt it away from a camera. What can you conclude about its true shape?
recall.why: A tilted circle projects to an oval; its actual shape need not change.
